title: Sparse R-CNN: End-to-End Object Detection with Learnable Proposals

problem.summary: Mainstream detectors depend on dense candidates (anchors, reference points, or RPN proposals), which forces NMS post-processing, many-to-one label assignment sensitive to heuristics, and heavy sensitivity to candidate design; DETR removes those components but each object query must interact with the whole image feature, so it converges slowly.
statements: Dense detectors produce redundant near-duplicate boxes, so NMS is a necessary post-processing component.
Many-to-one label assignment in training makes networks sensitive to heuristic assignment rules.
Final performance depends strongly on anchor sizes, aspect ratios, counts, reference-point density and proposal generation algorithms.
DETR's global image-context interaction per query slows training convergence and prevents a fully sparse pipeline.

evidence.quote: Such pipelines usually produce redundant and near-duplicate results, thus making non-maximum suppression (NMS) [1, 51] post-processing a necessary component.
The many-to-one label assignment problem [2, 58, 60] in training makes the network sensitive to heuristic assign rules.

DETR requires each object query to interact with global image context. This dense property not only slows down its training convergence [63], but also blocks it establishing a thoroughly sparse pipeline for object detection.

background.summary: The paper situates detectors along a dense to dense-to-sparse to sparse spectrum: anchor-based one-stage detectors, two-stage detectors whose RPN still scans dense candidates, DETR's set prediction, and earlier sparse work (G-CNN) plus concurrent Deformable DETR; sparse detection so far has trailed dense accuracy.

relatedWork.name: One-stage dense detectors
relatedWork.quote: One of mainstream pipelines is one-stage detector, which directly predicts the category and location of anchor boxes densely covering spatial positions, scales, and aspect ratios in a single-shot way, such as OverFeat [40], YOLO [36], SSD [31] and RetinaNet [29].

relatedWork.name: Two-stage detectors (Faster R-CNN)
relatedWork.relation: dense-to-sparse baseline whose RPN is replaced
relatedWork.quote: Two-stage detector is another mainstream pipeline and has dominated modern object detection for years [2, 6, 13, 14, 37].

relatedWork.name: DETR
relatedWork.relation: prior end-to-end set-prediction method, but not purely sparse
relatedWork.quote: Recently, DETR [3] is proposed to directly output the predictions without any hand-crafted components, achieving promising performance.

relatedWork.name: G-CNN
relatedWork.relation: precursor sparse detector with hand-designed grid prior
relatedWork.quote: G-CNN [34] can be viewed as a precursor to this group of algorithms.

relatedWork.name: Deformable DETR
relatedWork.relation: concurrent work restricting each query to local sampling points
relatedWork.quote: Concurrently, Deformable-DETR [63] is introduced to restrict each object query to attend to a small set of key sampling points around the reference points, instead of all points in feature map.

evidence.quote: Dense prior has always been cornerstone to success in detectors.
Sparse object detection has the potential to eliminate efforts to design dense candidates, but usually has trailed the accuracy of above dense detectors.

solution.summary: Sparse R-CNN replaces the RPN with a fixed set of N (default 100) learnable proposal boxes plus learnable proposal features; RoIAlign features are processed by a Dynamic Instance Interactive Head whose 1x1 convolution parameters are generated per proposal, iterated over six stages with self-attention and feature reuse, and trained with a one-to-one set prediction loss, yielding NMS-free end-to-end predictions.
solution.approach: Move from dense or dense-to-sparse detection to purely sparse detection by learning a small fixed set of proposals and conditioning each detection head on its own proposal feature instead of dense candidates and shared weights.
components: fixed sparse set of learnable proposal boxes (N x 4) replacing RPN candidates
learnable proposal features (N x 256) encoding instance characteristics
Dynamic Instance Interactive Head whose two 1x1 conv parameters come from the proposal feature
RoIAlign feature extraction for each proposal box
iterative cascade of 6 stages with self-attention and previous-stage feature reuse
set prediction loss with one-to-one bipartite matching (focal, L1 and GIoU terms)
FPN ResNet backbone with settings aligned to Faster R-CNN

evidence.quote: We present Sparse R-CNN, a purely sparse method for object detection in images.
a fixed sparse set of learned object proposals, total length of N , are provided to object recognition head to perform classification and location.
The parameters of these two convolutions are generated by corresponding proposal feature.
Set-based loss produces an optimal bipartite matching between predictions and ground truth objects.

experiments.summary: Trained with AdamW for 36 epochs (3x schedule) on COCO train2017 with 8 GPUs, Sparse R-CNN is compared against Detectron2 detectors and DETR-series models on val2017 and test-dev; ablations isolate learnable proposals, iterative architecture, feature reuse, dynamic head and initialization, plus proposal/stage counts; appendices cover CrowdHuman, self-supervised pre-training and transformer backbones.

evidence.quote: achieving 45.0 AP in standard 3× training schedule and running at 22 fps using ResNet-50 FPN model
The training convergence speed of Sparse R-CNN is 10× faster over DETR, as shown in Figure 2.

limitations.summary: Learnable proposals alone are useless (40.2 AP drops to 18.5 AP) and only work with the dynamic head and iterative feature reuse; a plain cascade adds no gain; accuracy saturates at 6 stages while more proposals and stages increase training time and reduce FPS.
items: Naively swapping RPN proposals for learnable boxes collapses AP from 40.2 to 18.5 without the iterative dynamic head.
A simple cascade architecture without feature reuse makes no big difference.
Beyond 6 stages performance is saturated while FPS drops from 23 to 17 and training time doubles.
Increasing proposals from 100 to 500 raises training time from 19h to 60h for small gains.

evidence.quote: The performance drops from 40.2 AP (Table 1 line 3) to 18.5 (Table 3).
However, we find that a simple cascade architecture does not make a big difference, as shown in Table 4.
Whereas, 500 proposals take much more training time, so we choose 100 and 300 as the main configurations.
Gradually increasing the number of stages, the performance is saturated at 6 stages.

futureDirections.direction: Rethink the necessity of dense priors in detectors and explore next-generation detector designs.
futureDirections.quote: We hope our work could inspire rethinking the necessary of dense prior in object detection and exploring next generation of object detector.

futureDirections.direction: Establish sparse detectors as a solid baseline to ease future research in the detection community.
futureDirections.quote: We hope sparse methods could serve as solid baseline and help ease future research in object detection community.

equations.name: Set prediction matching cost
equations.expr: L = λcls · Lcls + λL1 · LL1 + λgiou · Lgiou

deploymentClaims: Runs at 23 FPS with 100 proposals (22 FPS with 300) on NVIDIA Tesla V100
Inference needs no post-processing: the 100 predicted boxes are used directly without NMS

evidence.quote: Given an input image, Sparse R-CNN directly predicts 100 bounding boxes associated with their scores.
For evaluation, we directly use these 100 boxes without any post-processing.
The code is available at: https://github.com/PeizeSun/SparseR-CNN .
